title: Practice Overview
text:
This is a fictional training dataset created for an AI engineering take-home exercise. It does not contain real patient information and must not be used for clinical care.

EMER Aesthetic & Dermatology Center is a multi-service cosmetic dermatology and aesthetic medicine practice in West Hollywood, California. The practice provides consultations, injectable treatments, energy-based skin procedures, body-contouring services, acne and scar programs, skincare planning, and longitudinal follow-up.

The operating model emphasizes highly personalized treatment plans, photography and progress tracking, clear pre- and post-care instructions, coordinated follow-up, and a single longitudinal view of the patient. Staff roles include providers, nurses/medical assistants, coordinators, front desk, operations, marketing, and IT.

For this exercise, the knowledge system should distinguish between general practice information, procedure education, internal operating procedures, synthetic patient context, and versioned policies. Answers should identify the source records used rather than presenting unsourced conclusions.

title: AI Assistant Usage Policy
text:
The assistant is a decision-support and knowledge-retrieval system. It may summarize approved source material, answer operational questions, retrieve synthetic patient context, and explain general procedure information from this training corpus.

The assistant must not invent facts that are not supported by retrieved sources. When sources conflict, the most recent effective version marked as Current Policy should be preferred and the conflict should be disclosed. Patient-specific answers must cite the relevant synthetic patient record plus any procedure or policy source used.

The assistant must not claim to diagnose, prescribe, or replace a licensed clinician. For clinical-sounding questions, it should frame the answer as information found in the training corpus and recommend provider review where appropriate.

The assistant should preserve provenance. A useful response includes source titles or document IDs, especially for procedure, policy, and patient-specific questions.

title: Fractional Laser Resurfacing - General Overview
text:
Fractional laser resurfacing is used in this fictional practice to address selected concerns such as texture irregularity, visible photodamage, fine lines, and some types of acne scarring. Treatment depth, device settings, number of sessions, and candidacy are provider decisions.

Common planning considerations include skin type, recent sun exposure, active infection, history of abnormal scarring, current medications, recent procedures, and the patient's tolerance for downtime. The provider reviews risks, benefits, expected recovery, and alternatives before treatment.

Typical short-term effects may include redness, warmth, swelling, dryness, and temporary sensitivity. Patients are instructed to follow the individualized post-care plan, avoid picking or aggressive exfoliation, use gentle cleansing and approved moisturization, and follow the practice's sun-protection guidance.

This dataset intentionally does not provide device settings, treatment parameters, prescriptions, or patient-specific medical instructions.

title: RF Microneedling - General Overview
text:
Radiofrequency microneedling combines controlled microneedling with radiofrequency energy. In this fictional practice it may be considered for selected patients seeking improvement in texture, acne scarring, skin laxity, or other provider-approved concerns.

Before treatment, the provider considers current skin condition, history of pigment change or scarring, active infection, implanted devices where relevant, medications, and recent procedures. Treatment parameters are determined only by the licensed treating provider.

Expected short-term effects can include redness, mild swelling, pinpoint crusting, tenderness, and temporary dryness. Patients receive individualized aftercare, including gentle skincare, avoidance of unnecessary irritation, and sun protection.

The knowledge assistant should describe this procedure only at a general educational level and should not recommend parameters or treatment depth.

title: IPL / Photofacial - General Overview
text:
Intense pulsed light (IPL) is a light-based treatment commonly used for selected pigment and vascular concerns. Appropriate candidacy depends on skin tone, recent sun or tanning exposure, medications, active skin conditions, and the specific target.

The fictional practice requires provider review before treatment. Patients should disclose recent sun exposure, self-tanner use, new medications, and any history of unusual reactions to light-based procedures.

Short-term effects may include redness, warmth, temporary darkening of treated pigment, or mild swelling. The practice emphasizes sun protection and following individualized post-care instructions.

The assistant should not infer that IPL is appropriate for every pigmentation concern and should direct candidacy questions to a provider.

title: Neuromodulator Treatment - General Overview
text:
Neuromodulator injections are used for selected dynamic facial lines and other provider-approved aesthetic indications. Product choice, dose, injection sites, and candidacy are determined by the licensed provider.

The consultation reviews the patient's goals, prior response, relevant medical history, medications, asymmetry, and desired degree of movement. The practice documents baseline appearance and treatment areas.

Patients are advised that onset and duration vary. Follow-up may be scheduled when clinically appropriate to assess symmetry, response, and patient satisfaction.

This dataset does not provide dosing, injection maps, or medical directives.

title: Dermal Filler - General Overview
text:
Dermal fillers may be used to restore volume, refine contours, or address other provider-selected aesthetic goals. Product selection and placement depend on anatomy, tissue characteristics, treatment history, and patient goals.

The practice uses a consultation process that includes prior filler history, relevant medical history, treatment goals, photographs when appropriate, and discussion of expected benefits, limitations, alternatives, and complications.

Swelling, tenderness, bruising, and temporary asymmetry can occur after treatment. Urgent concerns are escalated to the treating provider according to practice policy.

The assistant may summarize general filler information but must not recommend injection sites, volumes, or products for a specific patient.

title: Biostimulatory Injectable - General Overview
text:
Biostimulatory injectables are used in selected aesthetic treatment plans to support gradual tissue remodeling or collagen-related goals. Results are generally progressive rather than immediate.

The provider determines whether a biostimulatory injectable is appropriate based on anatomy, treatment goals, prior procedures, relevant health history, and product-specific considerations. The practice emphasizes realistic expectations and staged follow-up.

The assistant should distinguish biostimulatory treatments from immediate-volume fillers when answering educational questions.

title: Acne and Acne-Scar Program - General Overview
text:
The fictional acne and acne-scar program is structured as a longitudinal plan rather than a single procedure. The provider evaluates active acne, scar type, pigment change, current products and medications, prior treatments, tolerance for downtime, and patient priorities.

A plan may combine provider-directed medical management, skincare, chemical or energy-based procedures, scar-focused procedures, and scheduled reassessment. Not every modality is appropriate for every patient.

Progress tracking uses standardized photography, treatment history, patient-reported goals, and follow-up notes. The assistant should not collapse active-acne treatment and scar treatment into the same recommendation without supporting source context.

title: Body Contouring - General Overview
text:
Body-contouring services in this fictional practice are evaluated according to the patient's goals, anatomy, prior procedures, general health, and whether the concern is primarily skin laxity, localized volume, muscle definition, or another target.

The provider explains expected outcomes, limitations, recovery considerations, and whether multiple modalities or staged treatment may be appropriate. The assistant must not infer surgical candidacy or recommend device settings.

Progress is typically documented with measurements, standardized photographs, treatment history, and follow-up assessments.

title: Chemical Peel - General Overview
text:
Chemical peels are used at different strengths for selected concerns such as uneven tone, texture, acne-related issues, or photodamage. Peel selection is based on skin type, recent procedures, current products, medication history, and treatment goals.

The practice requires individualized pre-care and aftercare. Patients are advised to avoid picking peeling skin and to follow provider-approved skincare and sun-protection instructions.

The assistant should not recommend peel agents or concentrations for a specific patient.

title: Skincare Consultation - General Overview
text:
Skincare consultations review the patient's current routine, treatment goals, tolerance, sensitivities, recent procedures, and adherence. The aim is to create a simple routine the patient can follow consistently and to coordinate products with in-office procedures.

The practice favors clearly documented morning and evening routines, notes on product purpose, and follow-up when tolerance or goals change. Product selection is individualized by the treating team.

The assistant may explain the structure of a skincare plan but should avoid inventing product recommendations that are not present in the source data.

title: General Pre-Procedure Checklist
text:
For all elective aesthetic procedures, the fictional practice uses a standardized pre-procedure workflow:
1. Confirm patient identity and scheduled procedure.
2. Confirm provider evaluation and consent status.
3. Review allergies, relevant medications, recent procedures, and changes in health history.
4. Confirm required photographs or baseline documentation.
5. Confirm that procedure-specific preparation instructions were provided and acknowledged.
6. Escalate any new contraindication, medication change, infection, unexpected symptom, pregnancy status concern, or uncertainty to the treating provider.
7. Do not proceed based solely on an AI-generated answer.

The assistant may retrieve this checklist for workflow questions.

title: General Post-Procedure Communication
text:
Post-procedure communication should be concise, procedure-specific, and documented. Staff should confirm that the patient received written aftercare, understands how to reach the practice, and knows which symptoms warrant contacting the clinical team.

Routine questions can be answered from approved aftercare materials. New or worsening symptoms, signs of infection, severe pain, unexpected visual symptoms, rapidly progressive swelling, or other urgent concerns should be escalated to a licensed provider.

The assistant should not reassure away a concerning symptom. Its role is to retrieve the appropriate source and support escalation.

title: Patient Intake and Identity Workflow
text:
Every new patient should have one canonical identity in the practice system. Staff should search for an existing record before creating a new one. Matching may use name, date of birth, phone, email, and other approved identifiers.

Potential duplicates are not automatically merged by the AI assistant. They are flagged for staff review. The patient timeline should link appointments, communications, notes, photographs, consents, payments, and follow-up activities to the canonical identity.

When identity is uncertain, the system should display the competing records and ask for human confirmation.

title: Consultation Workflow
text:
A consultation generally moves through: intake completion, goal capture, baseline photography when appropriate, provider review, treatment-plan discussion, documentation, quote or financial discussion where applicable, consent planning, and follow-up task creation.

The consultation record should preserve who created each note or action and when. AI-generated summaries should be labeled as derived content and linked back to their source notes or transcripts.

Unfinished consultations should appear in an exception queue until required documentation is complete.

title: Follow-Up and Reactivation Workflow
text:
The practice uses follow-up tasks to prevent patients from being lost after consultations or procedures. A follow-up record includes owner, due date, reason, current status, related patient, and source event.

Examples include post-procedure check-ins, treatment-plan follow-up, missed appointment outreach, skincare tolerance check, and dormant-patient reactivation.

Automated reminders may be drafted by AI, but patient-facing communication should follow approved templates and channel permissions. Opt-out and do-not-contact status must be respected.

title: Communication Channel Policy
text:
The practice may communicate through phone, SMS, email, and approved platform messaging. Every communication should be associated with the correct patient or lead record when identity is known.

The system should preserve timestamp, sender, recipient, channel, delivery status, and relevant thread or campaign reference. AI-generated drafts should be distinguishable from sent communications.

Do-not-contact and channel-specific opt-out settings override marketing or reactivation workflows.

title: AI Answer Quality Standard
Appointment Cancellation Policy - Superseded
text:
Superseded policy, effective January 1, 2026 through June 30, 2026.

Routine appointments canceled with less than 24 hours' notice may be subject to a cancellation fee unless waived by management. This version is retained only to test version-aware retrieval.

title: Appointment Cancellation Policy - Current
text:
Current policy, effective July 1, 2026.

Routine appointments should be canceled or rescheduled at least 48 hours in advance when possible. Late-cancellation or no-show handling is determined by the current scheduling policy and may be waived by authorized staff. This version supersedes OPS-306-V1.

When asked about the cancellation window, the assistant should use this version and may mention that an older 24-hour policy was superseded.

title: Office Hours and Escalation
text:
Fictional standard office coverage is Monday through Friday, 8:00 AM to 6:00 PM Pacific Time, with limited Saturday coverage for selected appointments.

Operational emergencies outside normal coverage should follow the on-call escalation path. For technology incidents, the primary IT contact is alerted first, followed by the backup support pod if the incident is not acknowledged within the defined escalation window.

The assistant should distinguish clinical escalation from IT escalation and should not route a clinical concern to IT.

title: AI / IT Incident Triage
text:
For AI-platform incidents, the support workflow is:
1. Confirm whether the issue affects one user or the entire service.
2. Check application health, authentication, tool/MCP connectivity, model-provider status, queues, databases, and recent deployments.
3. Review structured logs and error traces without exposing unnecessary sensitive content.
4. Identify whether the failure is configuration, credential, integration, provider, application, or infrastructure related.
5. Restore the safest known working state or escalate to the responsible engineer.
6. Document the incident, timeline, root cause when known, remediation, and follow-up action.

Examples of monitored conditions include tool registration failures, "no MCP attached / no tools attached" states, authentication failures, queue backlog, database errors, provider timeouts, and elevated latency.

title: AI Platform Permission Model
text:
AI tools are permissioned by capability. Read, write, approval-required, and denied operations should be explicitly separated.

Example:
- Read: retrieve appointment, retrieve approved patient summary, check system health.
- Write: create an internal task or add an internal note when the user's role permits it.
- Approval required: send external communication, modify an appointment, or update patient-facing information.
- Denied to autonomous AI: delete records, modify user permissions, export bulk patient data, change security settings.

Security enforcement belongs in the application/API/tool layer. Prompt instructions are not a security boundary. Every privileged tool call should record user identity, tool, resource, action, timestamp, authorization result, and execution outcome.

title: Fictional Consultation Pricing Reference
text:
Fictional training values only. These are not EMER Medical's real prices.

New-patient aesthetic consultation: $250.
Skincare consultation: $150.
Deposit rules and procedure pricing are intentionally omitted from the corpus.

If the user asks for a procedure price not listed here, the assistant should say the corpus does not contain that price rather than inventing one.

title: Lead Status Definitions
text:
Lead statuses used in the fictional training system:
- New: inquiry received but not yet contacted.
- Contacted: staff reached the lead or made a documented attempt.
- Consult Scheduled: consultation date/time confirmed.
- Consult Completed: consultation occurred.
- Treatment Planned: a provider-approved plan exists and the patient is considering or scheduling.
- Converted: first paid treatment completed.
- Dormant: no active next step after the defined follow-up window.

Status changes should be event-driven and auditable.
